findings.passage: Yet in a decade of interviews about the films that went wrong, she has never described a set as a place where she was misled or left unprotected.
findings.problem: The absolute "never" is contradicted by opened sources in the evidence record, two of which the draft itself quotes or holds. Vogue 2026 (S01, quoted later in the draft): "I've had experiences where people feel forgotten or lost or not taken care of or not seen on set or just undervalued" is a description of sets where people were left uncared for. Variety, July 2025 (S45, unused): "I can't waste time on toxic sets anymore, or in situations that are not fun or fulfilling or healthy." Vanity Fair 2021 (S03, half-quoted): she trusted Gyllenhaal because "she knows what it feels like to not be handled with grace and with care," protection language cut from the draft's "not seen" quotation. L'Officiel 2024 (S05, unused): streaming bosses "don't trust creative people or artists," a grievance in trust vocabulary. And "I signed up to do a very different version of the film we ended up making" is a being-misled framing as naturally as a work-made-false one. The discriminator can survive as a weighting of content; it cannot survive as a claimed absence. The FAQ "Why isn't Dakota Johnson a Type 6?" repeats the same "never".
findings.acceptance_test: The lede and the Type 6 FAQ no longer claim she "never" describes being misled or unprotected. The discriminator section quotes or names the "not taken care of" (2026), "toxic sets" (2025) and "not handled with grace and with care" (2021) lines and states, in one or two sentences, why the Four reading still outweighs them (for example: the care she names is always care for others' expression, and the toxic-sets line is about collaboration, not betrayal), or concedes that it does not and lowers confidence. The "signed up to do a very different version" line is acknowledged as readable both ways.

findings.passage: She refuses the structures a security-seeker leans on: "I really don't have a method, and I don't want one" (Marie Claire, 2020); rules are "really ridiculous, silly and stupid" (Bustle, 2024) and "really tough for me" (Vogue, 2026). Six theory predicts fear managed through preparation, allies and authority; Four theory predicts fear tolerated for the sake of feeling and being seen. Her stated overrides fit the second. Counterphobic Sixes also charge at fear, so this tilts the case rather than closing it; she frames the charge as curiosity and expression, never as defiance of the fear itself.
findings.problem: The draft names the counterphobic Six as its live alternative and then argues against the phobic Six. Rejection of rules, method and authority and charging at fear are the counterphobic Six's signature, so the "no method, no rules" lines are evidence for the named alternative, not against it; the evidence record's own C13 lists counterphobic Six first for exactly these lines. "Four theory predicts fear tolerated for the sake of feeling and being seen" is not a standard Four prediction; Four is a heart type whose theory predicts identity and depth-of-feeling motives, not a stance toward fear. "Never as defiance of the fear itself" is contradicted two sections earlier by her own words, "I am a very defiant person. If somebody tells me I can't do something, I am shaking, even if I had no interest in doing that thing," a defiance framing with no expression content, and by "I can see this world, so I just won't let anybody else do it," which is refusal-to-cede framing as much as vision. The Bustle exaggeration caveat lowers that line's weight; it cannot support "never".
findings.acceptance_test: The rule and method refusals are removed from the anti-Six column or explicitly labeled as consistent with the counterphobic Six. The paragraph restates the discriminator in terms the counterphobic variant actually predicts (defiance aimed at the authority or the fear versus expression aimed at the work and the self), weighs the Bustle defiance line and "I just won't let anybody else do it" inside that test rather than in another section, drops "never," and says plainly that her overrides are mixed (curiosity, vision, refusal to be told).

findings.passage: A Six's injury usually fuses fear and grievance into one figure, the authority who misled her or left her exposed. In the one passage where her fear and her grievance meet, Vanity Fair in 2022, she separates them herself: the fear attaches to the contract and the scenes, the praise to James and to how she and Dornan were treated, and the complaint to which movie got made.
findings.problem: The discriminator is built by narrowing Six grievance to betrayal ("misled or left exposed") and Four grievance to "work made false," then finding the Vanity Fair passage fits the second. Six theory, and the counterphobic variant in particular, also predicts grievance against an authority that imposes its will illegitimately, and the same passage is a textbook version of that story: an author with "creative control, all day, every day" who "demanded that certain things happen," met by covert resistance (two sets of takes, overnight rewrites of her own dialogue) and the retrospective verdict "this is psychotic." Taylor-Johnson's "Her vision versus mine" describes an authority contest too. The draft reads only the content of the complaint (contrivance, expression) and never tests its structure (illegitimate authority resisted covertly). An Eight reading of the same structure (control contested) is also unaddressed here, though the Eight section handles it elsewhere. The theoretical sentence about what a Six's injury "usually" does is asserted without source and is the load-bearing premise.
findings.acceptance_test: The section sets the counterphobic-Six reading of the Vanity Fair passage (illegitimate authority, covert resistance, "psychotic") beside the Four reading, and names the observation in her wording that tips it, for example that she never disputes James's right to control the films and that the complaint that survives is contrivance rather than being overruled. If no tipping observation exists, the section says the passage is inconclusive and the confidence drops to low. The "usually fuses" sentence is either sourced to a named Enneagram source or rewritten as this profile's own test.

findings.passage: Her self-definition has the same content as her grievance. In 2017, "different is what I'm about."
findings.problem: The Four case rests mostly on "different," "authentic" and "seen" vocabulary the draft itself concedes is industry-standard, plus two emotional-intensity lines (2017 "heartbroken all the time," 2026 summer camp). The Four's actual motivational core (not belonging, something wrong with me, meaning-making, self-reproach) is argued only by paraphrase while the record holds dated first-person lines that speak to it directly and were dropped at the draft stage: Bustle 2024 "I don't know if I'm from anywhere or I belong anywhere... So, yes, I do relate to the alien"; Vogue 2017 "I was a disaster, and I thought for so long that there was something wrong with my brain. Now I realize that it just works in a different way"; Vanity Fair 2022 "if I didn't try and apply great meaning to little things, I honestly don't think I'd make it"; Bustle 2024 "Most days I feel like the most useless piece of sh*t." Without them the Four argument could describe any indie-minded actor who dislikes studio notes, which is the standard's Enneagram-6 anchor failure in a different costume.
findings.acceptance_test: At least two of those dated lines appear in the Four case with the depression caveat the draft already uses, so the Four reading rests on identity, belonging and meaning evidence and not only on "different" and "seen." The lines are added without exceeding the word ceiling (cut elsewhere if needed).

findings.passage: On why she took _Fifty Shades_: "I'm a sexual person, and when I'm interested in something, I want to know so much about it," and, "That's why I did those big naked movies." (Vanity Fair, 2022)
findings.problem: This line is curiosity and appetite, which the draft's own Seven section treats as Seven's language, not identity or being seen. Calling nudity "a choice of exposure" to file it under Four overrides is a stretch, and it is the only override in the list that does not mention vision, feeling or being seen.
findings.acceptance_test: The line is either dropped from the override list or labeled as curiosity that does not discriminate between Four, Seven and counterphobic Six.

findings.passage: A Nine's even keel is hard to square with this, from 2017: "I think I'm a little bit heartbroken all the time, even when I'm in a happy relationship. I don't do casual very well, and my feelings, even the good ones, get so intense that they hurt."
findings.problem: The Nine dismissal rests on one nine-year-old self-report, while the record contains two Nine-shaped lines the draft does not surface: Marie Claire 2020, "I guess I have a lot of complexities, but they don't pour out of me. I don't make it anyone else's problem," and Bustle 2024, "I will accept and accommodate everyone's feelings and ideas and thoughts. I'll listen to everyone and take everything very seriously and then I will do what feels really right to me," which is accommodate-then-quietly-do-your-own-thing (the evidence record's C13 flags it as Nine). Containing intense feeling so it is nobody else's problem is as compatible with a Nine as with a Four.
findings.acceptance_test: The Nine paragraph quotes or names the 2020 "don't pour out of me" line and the 2024 accommodate-then-decide line, and names what still separates her from Nine with evidence already in the draft (the on-air Ellen correction, feathers ruffling at "cool," the fight she picked over which film got made).

findings.passage: Against it, she keeps puncturing her own image where winning happens: she doesn't "make sense" in the superhero world, shrugs at "tiny movies that didn't do well," and would accept a small Italian film as her last.
findings.problem: Self-deprecation on a press tour is itself an image strategy (the evidence record's C155 alternative says so), and her candor became a bankable persona (The Ringer's February 2024 "No One Is Safe From a Dakota Johnson Press Tour," S38, retained in research as the Three caveat). The Three test does not mention either, so the closer image-type contest (4 with a 3 wing versus 3 with a 4 wing) is never named, and a Three reader would find the puncturing evidence easy to absorb.
findings.acceptance_test: One or two sentences acknowledge that self-deprecation and viral candor can be image management, and name the observation that still separates her from Three (a decade of grievances aimed at contrivance rather than at reception, "Who cares?" about flops, accepting a small film as her last), or state that Four and Three are not cleanly separable on this record.

protected_passages.passage: Not that she was good, or that she had arrived. That she did something different.
protected_passages.reason: A small, dated self-report read for its exact wording; the kind of discriminator-grade detail the Four case needs more of.

protected_passages.passage: Still, on her talk of fear and safety alone, the Six reading would win.
protected_passages.reason: An honest concession that states exactly where the Four lead rests; rare in typing writing and it makes the rest of the argument trustworthy.

protected_passages.passage: A Seven's appetite usually runs from that sentence. Hers runs toward it.
protected_passages.reason: A crisp, evidence-based discriminator built from one quotation's second half; model for how the other alternatives should be closed.

protected_passages.passage: The Easter Bunny line puts safety at the end of the sentence and moviemaking in its service.
protected_passages.reason: Counterevidence conceded on its own terms rather than explained away; keep this habit through the repairs.

protected_passages.passage: If one does, its shape will matter: a fight framed as being misled or left unprotected would point toward Six, one framed as the work made false toward Four.
protected_passages.reason: Gives the reader an observable future test for the contested typing. Its distinctive contribution is the reopen signal; the Six side of the signal should widen to include a fight framed as resisting an illegitimate authority (see enneagram-03), but the sentence's function must survive.

assessment: The type argument is unusually honest about its limits: the Six case is given in full, the childhood is not used as cause, depression is excluded from typing, no wings or arrows are used to absorb contradictions, and the 60-word answer and metadata match the medium-confidence call. The discriminator itself is where it is weakest. It narrows Six grievance to betrayal and then reports that betrayal is absent, while opened sources hold protection- and trust-shaped lines ("not taken care of," "toxic sets," "not handled with grace and with care," "don't trust creative people") that the draft omits or trims; it names the counterphobic Six as the rival and then counts counterphobic behavior (rule refusal, defiance, charging at fear) against Six; and it reads only the content of the Vanity Fair passage, never its structure as an authority resisted covertly. The Four case, meanwhile, leans on brand vocabulary while dated lines about not belonging, something wrong with my brain, meaning-making and self-reproach sit unused in the record. Medium confidence is defensible only if the repairs in enneagram-01 through 04 hold; if the Vanity Fair passage proves inconclusive once the authority-resistance reading is tested, the honest call is low confidence or a Four-versus-Six split, not a thesis change on this record. Similarity diagnostic: every tripped pair is a self-match against the earlier same-subject draft; the cross-subject maximum is 0.053 with no shared phrases, so no formulaic reuse was found. Risks copied from the evidence record; no escalation beyond the contested typing already flagged.
